explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   • This is a full-stack, multi-component Haskell “monorepo” implementing:  
     – A 2D programming game engine (Swarm)  
     – A domain-specific language (DSL) for robot programs  
     – Scenario and topography libraries to describe worlds  
     – Multiple front-ends (CLI game, TUI, web UI, tournament server)  
     – Developer tools (doc generator, editor plugins, scripts)  
   • The README describes Swarm as a 2D resource-gathering game with programmable robots.

2. Break down the file structure into logical components  
   A. Core libraries (in src/)  
     • swarm-util: shared utilities (JSON/YAML, graph, lens, etc.)  
     • swarm-scenario: scenario definitions, parsing, validation  
     • swarm-topography: world layout, navigation, structure recognition  
     • swarm-engine: heart of the game loop, robot execution, achievements, scoring  
     • swarm-lang: DSL for writing robot programs (parser, typechecker, LSP)  
     • swarm-doc: documentation generator for commands & schema  
     • swarm-tournament: back-end logic for tournament server (REST API, DB)  
     • swarm-tui: terminal UI front-end  
     • swarm-web: web UI rendering & server  
   B. Executables (in app/)  
     • app/game: the main Swarm game CLI (invokes engine + UI layer)  
     • app/tournament: tournament server front end  
     • app/scene, app/doc: support tools (scene renderer, doc CLI)  
   C. Static assets and data  
     • data/: YAML scenario files, JSON schemas, text resources, images  
     • web/, tournament/web/: static HTML/JS/CSS for front-end UIs  
   D. Developer tooling  
     • scripts/: build, test, CI automation, normalization scripts  
     • editors/: Emacs, Vim, VSCode integrations  
     • test/: unit, integration, benchmark suites  

3. Examine inter-component relationships  
   • Core libraries form a layered dependency graph:  
     swarm-util ← swarm-scenario ← swarm-engine ← app/game  
     swarm-util ← swarm-scenario ← swarm-lang ← app/game  
     swarm-util ← swarm-scenario ← swarm-topography ← swarm-engine  
     …and so on for doc, tournament, tui, web  
   • Data files (YAML, JSON) are loaded at runtime by swarm-scenario or engine.  
   • app/game chooses a UI: TUI (via swarm-tui) or web UI (via swarm-web).  
   • Tournament server (app/tournament) exposes REST endpoints, persists to SQLite.  
   • Editor plugins and LSP server (in swarm-lang) communicate via Language Server Protocol.  

4. Key architectural patterns and principles  
   • Modular library design: small focused Haskell packages, each with clear responsibilities  
   • Layered dependencies: util → scenario → language/engine → front ends  
   • Data-driven world definitions: YAML scenarios + JSON schemas  
   • Pluggable UIs: swap TUI, web, or headless modes  
   • CLI + server executables all composed from core libraries  

5. Drawing the system design diagram  
   a. Components (boxes)  
     – Core libraries (group these in one area): swarm-util, swarm-scenario, swarm-topography, swarm-engine, swarm-lang, swarm-doc  
     – Front-end libraries: swarm-tui, swarm-web, swarm-tournament  
     – Executables: app/game (Swarm CLI), app/tournament (tournament server), app/doc, app/scene  
     – Data store: data/ folder, JSON schema files  
     – Database: SQLite for tournament  
     – Static web assets: web/, tournament/web/  
     – Developer tools and editor integrations (scripts/, editors/)  
     – External services: none beyond SQLite, static web host, GitHub CI  

   b. Relationships and data flow (arrows)  
     – Arrows from util → scenario → engine → app/game  
     – Arrow from scenario → lang → app/game  
     – Arrow from engine → tui and engine → web  
     – Arrow from tournament lib → app/tournament → SQLite  
     – Arrow from web UI assets → browser  
     – Arrow from LSP server → editor plugins → user’s editor  

   c. Architectural patterns to highlight  
     – Layered architecture: core (util, scenario) at bottom; engine + language in middle; UIs and servers at top  
     – Data-driven configuration: scenario files feed into scenario library  
     – DSL pipeline: Parser → AST → Typechecker → Interpreter in swarm-lang, then into engine  
     – REST API layer in tournament server  

   d. Technologies and frameworks  
     – Haskell + Cabal for core code  
     – YAML & JSON for scenario definitions and schemas  
     – SQLite for persistent tournament data  
     – JavaScript (Pixi.js) + HTML/CSS for web UI  
     – ANSI/Terminal for TUI  
     – Language Server Protocol for editor integrations  

6. Tailoring guidelines for this project  
   • Full-stack Haskell project: separate backend libraries (util, scenario, engine, lang) from front ends (game CLI, TUI, web, tournament).  
   • Emphasize data layer: scenario files and JSON schemas that drive game logic.  
   • For the tournament server: show the REST API boundary and the SQLite database.  
   • For the web UI: show static assets and how they fetch data from the Haskell back end.  
   • For the DSL: depict the pipeline (parser → type-checker → evaluator) feeding into the game engine.  

7. Diagramming conventions  
   – Use clear, descriptive labels on each box.  
   – Draw directional arrows for “depends on” or “calls into” relationships.  
   – Color-code by component type:  
     • Libraries (e.g., blue rectangles)  
     • Executables/servers (e.g., green)  
     • Data stores/files (e.g., yellow)  
     • Scripts/plugins (e.g., gray)  
   – Use different shapes (e.g., cylinders for databases, documents for file systems).  
   – Provide a legend explaining colors/shapes.  

By following these steps and capturing every core library, executable, data source, and their interactions, you will have a detailed and accurate system-design diagram specific to the Swarm project.  
</explanation>
